children: 1008 GMT - The U.S. has so far benefited from both the dollar and Treasurys being safe havens regardless of fiscal concerns but this could now change, DNB Asset Management's Ingvild Borgen says in a note. "To date, the U.S. has benefited from the fact that both its currency and its government bonds are regarded as the ultimate safe havens in global financial markets," the portfolio manager says. "The U.S. has not faced the market discipline that typically accompanies irresponsible fiscal policy--a pressure long experienced by countries in Europe and emerging markets." One potential positive is that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has already suggested that the U.S. will be compelled to take measures to prevent the debt burden from continuing to rise, Borgen says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0939 GMT - The recent rise in long-term U.S. Treasury yields isn't a cause for concern but the debt situation is becoming increasingly unsustainable, DNB Asset Management's Ingvild Borgen says in a note. DNB attributes the rise in yields to a combination of strong economic growth, sharp increase in the supply of highly-rated long-term bonds, greater uncertainty regarding inflation and a normalization of term premiums. "However, it is undeniable that the debt situation in the U.S. appears increasingly unsustainable," the portfolio manager says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0937 GMT - A resilient economy and robust bank lending has prompted estimates of the eurozone's neutral interest rate--when monetary policy neither restricts nor stimulates economic growth--to edge up over the last couple of years, Goldman Sachs economists Sven Jari Stehn and Alexandre Stott say in a note. "The average of three model estimates we track has increased by 19 basis points since late 2023," they say. That lowers the threshold for the European Central Bank to raise its key interest rate above the 2.5% terminal rate Goldman forecasts, and allows the ECB to sustain rates at a slightly higher level than its 2% long-run forecast, the economists say. Investors expect the ECB on Thursday to raise its policy rate to 2.5% from 2.25%. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0932 GMT - U.K. inflation is expected to rise to 3.3% in August, from 2.9% a month prior, RSM UK's Thomas Pugh says in a note. Still, this is unlikely to prompt a rate hike by the Bank of England, with price growth driven largely by higher motor fuel prices and airfares, he says. Inflation will likely keep rising, peaking close to 4% in 2027. "For Chancellor Healey, it will mean balancing an even bigger hit to his fiscal headroom against demands to do more on the cost of living," Pugh says. This will also keep the BOE on edge. "But the weaker labour market should limit any second-round effects, giving the [Monetary Policy Committee] enough room to stay on hold this year," he says. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

0927 GMT - Concerns about inflation risk due to elevated energy prices could dominate the U.K. government bonds market for a long time, Mizuho's Evelyne Gomez Liechti says in a note. Brent crude price advances 2.7% to $100.53 per barrel, raising inflation risk and the possibility of the Bank of England increasing interest rates in the coming months. Markets fully price in three quarter-point BOE rate rises by July 2027, LSEG data show. Ten-year gilt yields climb 4 basis points to last trade at 5.202%, Tradeweb data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0923 GMT - The cost of insuring euro-denominated credit against default rises due to reduced risk appetite as U.S.-Iran hostilities intensify. The U.S. destroyed Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to Iran's attempts to strike U.S. warships. Renewed tensions caused oil prices to climb above $100 per barrel and lowered appetite for risk. The iTraxx Europe Crossover index of euro high-yield credit default swaps rises 2 basis points to 253bps, a three-week high, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0916 GMT - Industrial production in France stumbled in July, adding to downside risk for overall eurozone manufacturing after the decline in German reported earlier this week, Pantheon Macroeconomics' Claus Vistesen. Output dropped 0.4% on month at the start of the third quarter, below consensus of a small increase, after a downwardly revised 0.1% decline in June. The decline was broad-based, but propelled by transport equipment. Production there dropped 2.8%, extending June's decline, "indicating that the otherwise solid upturn in aerospace output--which boosted industry in the second quarter--is now coming off the boil," Vistesen says. The better news is that business surveys still look decent, after a rebound in August's manufacturing output PMI and with the Insee production index holding up, he says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0847 GMT - China's 2026 economic growth forecast remains intact, but growth will likely slow in the medium term, BofA Securities says in a research note. BofA keeps its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 4.5% in view of remaining policy room and policymakers' strong will to meet the growth target this year, the bank says. "Despite flashing red lights in domestic demand, supply side production will likely decelerate only gradually, limiting the extent of growth deceleration in the near future," they note. However, the bank expects the Chinese economy's growth to slow to 4.2% in 2027 and 4.0% in 2028. This is mainly due to headwinds for domestic activities and delayed policy easing, BofA says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0846 GMT - Markets await the U.S. Treasury's communication on the size of the long-dated bonds buyback operation due to be announced on Wednesday, which could offer some temporary relief to long-dated Treasurys, Mizuho's Evelyne Gomez-Liechti says in a note. Treasury announced in August that purchases of long-dated bonds would at least double starting in September. A sizeable announcement could temporarily support long-end Treasurys, although the impact is unlikely to last given inflation concerns from high oil prices, Gomez-Liechti says. U.S. 30-year Treasury yields fall 1.4 basis points to last trade at 5.250% ahead of the announcement, Tradeweb data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0821 GMT - China's export strength has proven to be a "double-edged sword" for China's economy, according to BofA Securities in a research note. "On the one hand, robust external demand has provided a critical buffer against weak domestic demand, helping keep overall growth on track to meet the lower bound of the government's 4.5% growth target," the bank says. However, persistently strong export performance, has reduced the urgency for policymakers to deliver additional easing measures, BofA says. Policymakers has refrained from announcing fresh stimulus at the July Politburo meeting, opting instead to emphasize more effective implementation of existing policies, they say. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0812 GMT - The won's strength against the dollar could moderate underlying inflation in South Korea, says Citigroup economist Jin-Wook Kim. If the local currency strengthens by 10% against the greenback, core inflation would fall by around 0.35 percentage point over a year, Kim writes in a note. He expects the Bank of Korea to hold the policy rate steady at the coming October meeting after two consecutive rate increases in July and August to curb inflationary pressure. Citi maintains its earlier view that the BOK would raise interest rates by 25 basis points each in November 2026 and February 2027, he adds. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0757 GMT - The unusual trend of the yuan gaining while Chinese government bond yields fall has further room to run, Capital Economics' Thomas Mathews says in a note. The recent market moves, though unusual, reflect China's economic situation: while the trade surplus is huge, warranting a stronger exchange rate, sluggish domestic demand calls for looser financial conditions, such as lower bond yields, he says. While Mathews thinks the trend has further room to run, there could be some near-term stumbling blocks, as the People's Bank of China is seeking to stymie the yuan's appreciation through its setting of the daily fix, and China's fiscal policy looks set to be more expansionary. (sherry.qin@wsj.com)
